\chapter{Water, Wine, and Bread}
\label{ch:la-water-wine-bread}

This chapter is generated from the canonical micro-lessons used by Language Ladder.
Each section stays independently resumable and preserves the authored prerequisite order.

\section[aqua, vīnum]{aqua, vīnum — one word worn thin, one word untouched}

\label{lesson:LA-C10-aqua-vinum}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} Two everyday Latin nouns — and two wildly different fates. One of Rome's daughters wore this word down to almost nothing. The other word barely moved at all, anywhere.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{aqua, aquae} — "\textbf{water}." Spanish and Italian kept it close to whole: \textbf{agua}, \textbf{acqua}. French, though, eroded it further than almost any other Latin word in this course: \emph{aqua $\to$ ewe $\to$ eaue $\to$ \textbf{eau}} — three written letters, \emph{e-a-u}, spelling one bare vowel sound, "oh." Compare \emph{caput}, which French similarly abandoned as an everyday word (for \emph{testa}) — \emph{aqua} wasn't replaced, but it was worn down almost to nothing while staying in place.

English kept the \textbf{whole, undamaged} word as a learned borrowing: \textbf{aquatic, aquarium, aqueduct, aqualung} all sound exactly like their Latin ancestor.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: vīnum — survived, everywhere, almost untouched}
\textbf{vīnum, vīnī} — "\textbf{wine}." Unlike \emph{aqua} and \emph{caput}, this word simply \textbf{didn't erode much in any direction}: Spanish \emph{vino}, French \emph{vin}, Italian \emph{vino} — all close to the original. Germanic borrowed it directly and early, giving English \textbf{wine} itself. Centuries later, English picked up more of the family — this time secondhand, through \textbf{French}: \textbf{vine} (< OF \emph{vigne} < \emph{vīnea}, "vineyard"), \textbf{vinegar} (< OF \emph{vinaigre}, \emph{vin} + \emph{aigre}, ultimately \emph{acer} "sour"), \textbf{vintage} (< OF \emph{vendage} < \emph{vīndēmia}, \emph{vīnum} + \emph{dēmere} "to harvest"). \textbf{Vineyard} isn't a borrowing at all — English built it at home, compounding the already- borrowed "wine" with native "yard." Few Latin words traveled this far, by this many different roads, and stayed this recognizable.

\subsection*{Guided Practice}
{[}PAUSE 1s{]}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "aqua" — water — then the daughters: "agua, acqua, eau"{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "vīnum" — wine — then: "vino, vin, vino, wine"{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: the contrast — aqua wore thin in French; vīnum stayed solid everywhere{]}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Wrap-up recall}]
{[}PAUSE 3s{]} Which Latin word for a drink got worn down almost to nothing, and in which language? (\textbf{Aqua}, in \textbf{French} — down to a bare "eau.") Which word barely changed \textbf{anywhere}, surviving into every Romance daughter and into English too? (\textbf{Vīnum} — wine, vino, vin, vino.) Where did the \emph{whole}, undamaged form of \emph{aqua} survive in English? (\textbf{Aquatic, aquarium, aqueduct} — learned borrowings, not everyday words.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pānis]{pānis — bread, and the friend who shares it}

\label{lesson:LA-C10-panis}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} One Latin word for bread, surviving whole across every Romance daughter — and hiding, inside a compound, one of the loveliest word-stories in English.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{pānis, pānis} — "\textbf{bread}." Spanish \textbf{pan}, French \textbf{pain}, Italian \textbf{pane} all continue it directly — bread mattered enough to keep its own name everywhere.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: com- + pānis — "sharing bread"}
Add the prefix \textbf{com-} ("with, together") and you get \textbf{compānio/ compānia} — a Vulgar Latin coinage, not a Classical-era word — literally "\textbf{one you share bread with}," the direct ancestor of English \textbf{companion} and \textbf{company}. A \emph{company} was, at first, nothing more than a group who ate together.

\begin{culture}
English only kept the \textbf{friendship} half of this word — \emph{companion} has nothing to do with actual bread anymore to an English speaker. \textbf{Spanish}, though, still keeps \textbf{both halves} traceably related: \textbf{pan} (the bread itself) and \textbf{compañero} (the friend, "one who shares \emph{pan}") sit right next to each other in the same language, both transparently built from the same root. Latin's \emph{pānis} split into two separate lives in English, but stayed one visible family in Spanish.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Guided Practice}
{[}PAUSE 1s{]}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "pānis" — bread — then "pan, pain, pane"{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "com- + pānis" — "with bread" — companion, company{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: the contrast — English kept only the friend; Spanish kept both the bread and the friend{]}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Wrap-up recall}]
{[}PAUSE 3s{]} What does \textbf{pānis} give Spanish, French, and Italian directly? (\textbf{Pan, pain, pane} — bread.) What English words come from \emph{com- + pānis}, and what do they literally mean? (\textbf{Companion, company} — "one you \textbf{share bread with}.") Does English still connect "companion" to actual bread? (\textbf{No} — only Spanish keeps both \emph{pan} and \emph{compañero} traceably related.)
\end{tcolorbox}
